newsitem.title: UK: Hermes boss warns against scrapping UK tax credits.
newsitem.headline: Hermes boss warns against scrapping UK tax credits.

text.p: The head of Hermes, one of Britain's largest pension funds, on Friday warned the winner of next month's national election against scrapping tax credit on share dividends.

"If pension funds -- and for that mattter charities -- are unable to claim this tax back, their gross income on UK equities will fall by up to 20 percent," Alastair Ross Goobey, chief executive of Hermes Pensions Management, told Reuters.
Advance corporation tax (ACT) is payable by British tax resident companies on dividends but can be offset against their mainstream corporation tax liability.
Currently, institutions such as pension funds pay no tax and are able to generate extra income by claiming back the ACT paid by companies which distribute dividends net of basic tax.

Ross Goobey, who made his views known in a letter to the Financial Times, said any change to the system would lead to a fall in the value of pension funds, forcing companies to make up the difference under a law which comes into force this weekend.

He said that because the opposition Labour Party had ruled out changes to income tax, it was widely believed it would propose reducing the credit for corporation tax paid to non-taxpaying recipients of dividends, including pension funds.
But he warned that removing ACT relief would "have the effect of reducing the gross yield on equities from the current 3.7 percent to 2.96 percent".

Actuaries would immediately factor in a long-term fall in pension funds' gross income on about half of their assets. Schemes which thought they were adequately funded would find themselves at or below the requirements.

They would be required either to inject a large lump sum into their funds or increase employer contributions, which could be offset against corporation tax. This could in turn hit company cash flows, making the net effect on corporate tax revenues negligible, he argued.
Ross Goobey said it could also make British equities relatively less attractive compared with other assets, changing the relationship between the two.
Theoretically it could make an asset class such as property, on which pension funds get all their income gross, more attractive vis-a-vis British equities.
"This (change) will have a significant effect on the valuation of pension funds and force companies under the new pensions act to make up any deficit in fairly short order. And the sums are huge."
Hermes manages the British Telecommunications Plc and Post Office pension funds.

In its election manifesto, launched on Thursday, Labour promised a review of the corporate and capital gains tax regimes but otherwise gave little detail of its plans for the tax system, except to say reform would promote saving and investment.

"We will review the corporate and capital gains tax regimes to see how the law system can promote greater long term investment," said the party, which holds a wide lead over the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls.

British pension funds hold around 300 billion pounds ($491.9 billion) of British equities and they would lose about 1.8 billion pounds a year in income if the changes were brought in, Ross Goobey said.
While analysts agreed a change would have a detrimental effect on the British stock market, some said they did not see any change in prospect.
"I suspect there won't be any change to this regime," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at British stockbroking firm Charterhouse.

And while a change to the rules would knock share prices, it was impossible to assess by exactly how much. Jeffrey said that the last time a change had been made, there had been an immediate effect but that this had subsequently rebounded.
The Conservative government reduced ACT relief by five percentage points in 1993.

Although scrapping the tax relief on dividends would make British equities "slightly less attractive", Jeffrey said investors should be looking at the overall earnings of British companies rather than simply their dividend earnings.
"It would do some damage, but it's easy to exaggerate the damage that would be done," he added.
